q-36378.name: Question 1
q-36378.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=2x+4y+5xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,1).$
q-36378.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+4y+5xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+4y+5xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(5y+2)\text{ }i+(5x+4)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(5\cdot 1+2)\text{ }i+(5\cdot 2+4)\text{ }j \\  & =7i+14j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(2,1)}{‖∇f(2,1)‖} & =\frac{7i+14j}{\sqrt{{7}^{2}+(14)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{7i+14j}{7\sqrt{5}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}(i+2\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

q-36311.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,1).$
q-36311.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =(4x+0-0)\,i+(0+4y-1)\,j \\  & =4x\,i+(4y-1)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =4(0)\,i+(4(1)-1)\,j \\  & =3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(0,1):$

$$
\frac{∇f(0,1)}{‖∇f(0,1)‖}=\frac{3\,j}{3}=j
$$

q-71370.name: Question 3
q-71370.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$
q-71370.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$, can be found by computing $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j \\ ∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) & =2(-\frac{1}{2})\text{ }i+2(\frac{1}{2})\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})}{‖∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})‖} & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

q-71374.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=x+3y-2xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1).$
q-71374.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(1-2y)\text{ }i+(3-2x)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(\frac{3}{2},1) & =(1-2(1))\text{ }i+(3-2(\frac{3}{2}))\text{ }j \\  & =-i\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(\frac{3}{2},1)}{‖∇f(\frac{3}{2},1)‖} & =\frac{-i}{1}=-i\end{aligned}
$$

q-71381.name: Question 5
q-71381.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}+x+y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,0).$
q-71381.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,0)$, can be found by computing $∇f(0,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y}+x+y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y}+x+y)\text{ }j \\  & =({e}^{x+y}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y}+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,0) & =({e}^{0+0}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{0+0}+1)\text{ }j \\  & =2i+2j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(0,0)}{‖∇f(0,0)‖} & =\frac{2i+2j}{\sqrt{(2)^{2}+(2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2i+2j}{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

q-130723.name: Question 6
q-130723.problem: Consider the plane curve $4xy+2{x}^{2}=x+2y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$
q-130723.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side: 

$$
\begin{aligned}4xy+2{x}^{2} & =x+2y \\ 4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+2{x}^{2}-x-2y)\,j \\  & =(4y+4x-1)\,i+(4x-2)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(4(-1)+4(2)-1)\,i+(4(2)-2)\,j \\  & =3\,i+6\,j \\  & =⟨3,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨3,6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{3} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{6} \\ 6(x-2) & =3(y+1) \\ 2(x-2) & =y+1 \\ 2x-4 & =y+1 \\ 2x-y-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-71393.name: Question 7
q-71393.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)=2xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,1).$
q-71393.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-2y)\,i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-2x)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(0))\,j \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,1)=⟨-1,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1} & =\frac{y-1}{1} \\ -x & =y-1 \\ x+y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the plane curve ln⁡(x+y)=2xy. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (0,1).

a
−x+y−1=0
b
x−y+1=0
c
x+y−1=0

x+y+1=0
e
x+2y−2=0
Submit

If we set f(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y)−2xy, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (0,1) can be found by computing ∇f(0,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (0,1):

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(ln⁡(x+y)−2xy)i+∂∂y(ln⁡(x+y)−2xy)j=(1x+y−2y)i+(1x+y−2x)j∇f(0,1)=(10+1−2(1))i+(10+1−2(0))j=−i+j=⟨−1,1⟩

Hence, ∇f(0,1)=⟨−1,1⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (0,1).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−0−1=y−11−x=y−1x+y−1=0

q-36339.name: Question 8
q-36339.problem: Consider the plane curve $6xy=5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,1).$
q-36339.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,j \\  & =(10x-6y)\,i+(2y-6x)\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(10-6(1))\,i+(2(1)-6)\,j \\  & =4\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨4,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,1)=⟨4,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{4} & =\frac{y-1}{-4} \\ x-1 & =-y+1 \\ x+y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-71390.problem: Consider the plane curve ${y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}=4xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,-3).$
q-71390.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+3{x}^{2} & =4xy \\ {y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+3{x}^{2}-4xy)\,j \\  & =(6x-4y)\,i+(2y-4x)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,-3) & =(6(-1)-4(-3))\,i+(2(-3)-4(-1))\,j \\  & =6\,i-2\,j \\  & =⟨6,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,-3)=⟨6,-2⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{6} & =\frac{y-(-3)}{-2} \\ (-2)(x+1) & =6(y+3) \\ -2x-2 & =6y+18 \\ 6y+2x+20 & =0 \\ 3y+x+10 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (−1,−3) can be found by computing ∇f(−1,−3).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (−1,−3):

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(y2+3x2−4xy)i+∂∂y(y2+3x2−4xy)j=(6x−4y)i+(2y−4x)j∇f(−1,−3)=(6(−1)−4(−3))i+(2(−3)−4(−1))j=6i−2j=⟨6,−2⟩

Hence, ∇f(−1,−3)=⟨6,−2⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (−1,−3).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−(−1)6=y−(−3)−2(−2)(x+1)=6(y+3)−2x−2=6y+186y+2x+20=03y+x+10=0

q-71385.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$
q-71385.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=4.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =2(2)\,i+2(0)\,j \\  & =4\,i \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨4,0⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-2)0-(y-0)4 & =0 \\ -4y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-131116.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1).$
q-131116.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,k \\  & =3{x}^{2}\text{ }i+2{z}^{2}y\text{ }j+(2z{y}^{2}+2)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,-1) & =3(1)^{2}\,i+2(-1)^{2}(-1)\,j+(2(-1)(-1)^{2}+2)k \\  & =3\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $3\,i-2\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1).$

For the function f(x,y,z)=x3yz−xyz2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−2,1).

a
 −4i+2k
b
 4i−k
c
 −4i+2j+2k
d
 −2i−2j+k
e
 −2j+4k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−2,1) can be found by computing ∇f(1,−2,1).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(1,−1,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x3yz−xyz2)i+∂∂y(x3yz−xyz2)j+∂∂z(x3yz−xyz2)k=(3x2yz−yz2) i+(x3z−xz2) j+(x3y−2xyz) k∇f(1,−2,1)=(3(1)2(−2)(1)−(−2)(1)2)i+((1)3(1)−(1)(1)2)j+((1)3(−2)−2(1)(−2)(1))k=−4i+2k

Therefore, −4i+2k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−2,1).

q-65167.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}-2yz+z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1).$
q-65167.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$  and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}-2yz+z)\,k \\  & ={y}^{2}\text{ }i+(2xy-2z)\text{ }j+(-2y+1)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,1) & =(-1)^{2}\,i+(2(1)(-1)-2(1))\,j+(-2(-1)+1)\,k \\  & =1\,i-4j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $\,i-4\,j+3\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1).$

Question 15
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=ex+y+z+x+y+z, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(0,0,0).

a
2i+2j+2k
b
2i+j+2k
c
2i+2j+k
d
i+2j+2k
e
2i+j+k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(0,0,0) can be found by computing ∇f(0,0,0).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(0,0,0):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(ex+y+z+x+y+z)i+∂∂y(ex+y+z+x+y+z)j+∂∂z(ex+y+z+x+y+z)k=(ex+y+z+1) i+(ex+y+z+1) j+(ex+y+z+1) k∇f(0,0,0)=(e0+0+0+1)i+(e0+0+0+1)j+(e0+0+0+1)k=2i+2j+2k

Therefore, 2i+2j+2k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(0,0,0).

q-131124.name: Question 16
q-131124.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}={x}^{2}-6x+12$ at the point $(2,0,1).$
q-131124.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-6x \\ 4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x & =12\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=12.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(4{z}^{2}-4{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+6x)k \\  & =(6-2x)\,i-8y\,j+8z\,k \\ ∇f(2,0,1) & =(6-2(2))\,i-8(0)\text{ }j+8(1)\,k \\  & =2\,i+8\,k \\  & =⟨2,0,8⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(2,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(2,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨2,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(2,0,1)=⟨2,0,1⟩+t\,⟨2,0,8⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

q-37231.problem: Find parametric equations for the normal line to the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=1$ at the point $(0,0,\sqrt{e}).$
q-37231.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}).$ Then,  our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=1.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,0,\sqrt{e})$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,0,\sqrt{e}).$  

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,0,\sqrt{e}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}))k \\  & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\text{ }j+\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,\sqrt{e}) & =\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(\sqrt{e})^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(\sqrt{e})^{2}}\text{ }j+\frac{2\sqrt{e}}{(0)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(\sqrt{e})^{2}}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{e}}{e}k\end{aligned}
$$

The parametric equations for the normal line to $f(x,y,z)$ at a point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ are given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={x}_{0}+{f}_{x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})t, \\ y & ={y}_{0}+{f}_{y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})t, \\ z & ={z}_{0}+{f}_{z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametic equations  for the normal line to our surface that  passes through the point $(0,0,\sqrt{e})$ can be written as 
 

$$
x=0,\,y=0,\,z=\sqrt{e}+\frac{2t\sqrt{e}}{e}
$$

Question 17
?

Find parametric equations for the normal line to the surface ln⁡(x2+y2+z2)=1 at the point (0,0,e).

a
x=t, y=0, z=e+tee
b
x=0, y=t, z=e+2te
c
x=0, y=0, z=e+2tee
d
x=t, y=t, z=2tee
e
x=−t, y=0, z=e+tee
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's set f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x2+y2+z2). Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=1.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (0,0,e) can be found by computing ∇f(0,0,e).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (0,0,e):

∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x(ln⁡(x2+y2+z2))i+∂∂y(ln⁡(x2+y2+z2))j+∂∂z(ln⁡(x2+y2+z2))k=2xx2+y2+z2 i+2yx2+y2+z2 j+2zx2+y2+z2 k∇f(0,0,e)=2(0)(0)2+(0)2+(e)2 i+2(0)(0)2+(0)2+(e)2 j+2e(0)2+(0)2+(e)2 k=2eek

The parametric equations for the normal line to f(x,y,z) at a point (x0,y0,z0) are given by x=x0+fx(x0,y0,z0)t,y=y0+fy(x0,y0,z0)t,z=z0+fz(x0,y0,z0)t. Therefore, the parametic equations for the normal line to our surface that passes through the point (0,0,e) can be written as x=0,y=0,z=e+2tee

q-131125.name: Question 18
q-131125.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}-{y}^{2}=4-4z$ at the point $(0,2,2).$
q-131125.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =4-4z \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z & =4\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=4.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,2,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,2,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+4z)k \\  & =2x\,i-2y\,j+4\,k \\ ∇f(0,2,2) & =2(0)\,i-2(2)\text{ }j+4\,k \\  & =-4\,j+4\,k \\  & =⟨0,-4,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(0,2,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,2,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,2,2⟩+t\,∇f(0,2,2)=⟨0,2,2⟩+t\,⟨0,-4,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface x2−y2=4−4z at the point (0,2,2).

a

b

EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side:

x2−y2=4−4zx2−y2+4z=4

If we set f(x,y,z)=x2−y2+4z, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=4.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (0,2,2) can be found by computing ∇f(0,2,2).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (0,2,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2−y2+4z)i+∂∂y(x2−y2+4z)j+∂∂z(x2−y2+4z)k=2xi−2yj+4k∇f(0,2,2)=2(0)i−2(2) j+4k=−4j+4k=⟨0,−4,4⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(0,2,2) and passes through the point (0,2,2) can be written as

r=⟨0,2,2⟩+t∇f(0,2,2)=⟨0,2,2⟩+t⟨0,−4,4⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).

q-37232.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}=1$ at the point $(2,1,2).$
q-37232.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=1.$     

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1,2).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1,2):$    

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z})\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{2x}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }j-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2{x}^{2}+y-4z}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,2) & =\frac{2\cdot 2}{\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }j-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\cdot {2}^{2}+1-4\cdot 2}}\text{ }k \\  & =4\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j-2\text{ }k \\  & =⟨4,\,\frac{1}{2},\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{y-1}{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{z-2}{-2} \\ \frac{x-2}{4}=2y-2=\frac{2-z}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface 2x2+y−4z=1 at the point (2,1,2).

a
x−24=y−13=2−z2

Let's set f(x,y,z)=2x2+y−4z. Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=1.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (2,1,2) can be found by computing ∇f(2,1,2).

q-131126.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x=5$ at the point $(1,-1,2).$
q-131126.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=5.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)k \\  & =(2xy+{z}^{2})\,i+({x}^{2}+2yz)\,j+({y}^{2}+2zx)\,k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(2(1)(-1)+(2)^{2})\text{ }i+((1)^{2}+2(-1)(2))\text{ }j+((-1)^{2}+2(2)(1))\text{ }k \\  & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k \\  & =⟨2,-3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,-1,2)$ and passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,∇f(1,-1,2)=⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨2,-3,5⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Question 20
?

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface x2y+y2z+z2x=5 at the point (1,−1,2).

a
 ⟨1,−1,2⟩+t⟨−2,5,−3⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
 ⟨−2,5,−3⟩+t⟨1,−1,2⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
 ⟨1,−1,2⟩+t⟨4,5,−5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
 ⟨2,3,−5⟩+t⟨1,−1,2⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
 ⟨1,−1,2⟩+t⟨2,−3,5⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's set f(x,y,z)=x2y+y2z+z2x. Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=5.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (1,−1,2) can be found by computing ∇f(1,−1,2).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (1,−1,2):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2y+y2z+z2x)i+∂∂y(x2y+y2z+z2x)j+∂∂z(x2y+y2z+z2x)k=(2xy+z2)i+(x2+2yz)j+(y2+2zx)k∇f(1,−1,2)=(2(1)(−1)+(2)2) i+((1)2+2(−1)(2)) j+((−1)2+2(2)(1)) k=2i−3j+5k=⟨2,−3,5⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(1,−1,2) and passes through the point (1,−1,2) can be written as

r=⟨1,−1,2⟩+t∇f(1,−1,2)=⟨1,−1,2⟩+t⟨2,−3,5⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).
